questions.stem: A 49-year-old man planned to travel to India for 10 days in Delhi. He was healthy, did not take any medications, and reported he received all his vaccines as a child. His last Tdap was 3 years prior, and he received annual influenza vaccination. He worked in sales.
questions.lead_in: In addition to typhoid and hepatitis A, what vaccination should be recommended to this patient?
questions.explanation: MMR Vaccinations should be tailored to the patient based on previous vaccinations, specific trip, and risks. HAV and typhoid are endemic in India and should be given. The risk for Japanese encephalitis and rabies should be mentioned and discussed (mosquito precautions, avoidance of contact with animals), but the risk is very small in short-lasting trips limited to urban areas. HBV is endemic in India (intermediate/high prevalence) so vaccination should be considered, but is only recommended for those whose activities or medical history put them at increased risk (for example, healthcare workers, IDU, those who may have unprotected sex). For patients from the United States, MMR is indicated in those born in 1957 or later, without evidence of immunity or two doses of the live vaccine. MMR was given as a single dose before the 1990s, so in this case it is very likely that the patient has not received a second MMR dose. In the UK, individuals born before 1970 are likely to have had measles naturally, but MMR should be offered if they are considered to be at high risk of exposure, such as travel to areas with high incidence; those born between 1970 and 1979 should be offered MMR wherever feasible.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q45

needs: Chapter 313 — Infections in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man attended for pretravel advice. He had undergone heart transplantation 6 months previously. He was maintained on tacrolimus and prednisone for immunosuppression and had not had any episodes of allograft rejection. He intended to travel to Vellore, India, for 2 weeks and then on to Manila, the Philippines, for 2 weeks before returning home.
questions.explanation: Oral typhoid vaccine Immunosuppressed patients should not receive live vaccines such as BCG, MMR, oral polio, and oral typhoid vaccine. Inactivated vaccines such as influenza, hepatitis A or B, pneumococcal, and adsorbed tetanus vaccine are permitted, although these are less likely to be effective in immunocompromised hosts. Both oral and inactivated polio vaccine offer excellent individual immunity, but the oral vaccine is live and therefore contraindicated in this patient. Routine polio immunizations in both the UK and the United States are given as inactivated polio vaccine (IPV).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q41

needs: Chapter 313 — Infections in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients
questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman sought pretravel medical advice. She planned to go to Bolivia for vacation to visit family. She had a history of liver transplantation for Wilson’s disease 6 months prior and was doing well on immunosuppressants. She asked specifically about yellow fever vaccination.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Advise against future travel to Bolivia due to the risk of yellow fever
Counsel against the trip if visiting a high-risk area
Delay the travel plans until she is 2 years post-transplant
Mosquito bite avoidance precautions will suffice

questions.explanation: Counsel against the trip if visiting high-risk area This is an immunocompromised patient planning an elective trip to a country that has yellow fever. Yellow fever is a live vaccine that could cause significant side effects in immunosuppression. Areas with risk for yellow fever are geographically restricted and thus avoided. A review of the specific destinations can inform if the patient will be exposed to yellow fever or not.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q29

parts.text: List 4 malaria prophylaxis options including instructions on when to start and when to stop

cohort_answer.text: Chloroquine 500mg salt PO 1-2 weeks prior to leaving, then weekly while there, then continue weekly for 4 weeks after returning. Mefloquine 250mg salt PO weekly 2-3 weeks prior to leaving, weekly while away then for 4 weeks after returning. Atovaquone/proguanil 250mg/100mg PO daily 1-2 days before leaving, daily while away, then for 1 week after returning. Doxycycline 100mg PO daily 1-2 days before leaving, daily while away, then 4 weeks after returning

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action?
What do you need to know to know how efficacious it would be for each traveler?

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Live attenuated vaccine (oral cholera vaccine). Efficacy factors: Need to be given more than 10 days prior to administration of chloroquine; needs to be given at least 10 days prior to trip.
